result.topic_en: This spread covers pp. 258–259. It finishes Euler's tables listing, for primes N of the forms 8n±1 and 8n±3, a power 2^n±1 that N divides. It then states, without proof, the theorem that a prime 2p+1 of form 8n±1 divides 2^p−1 and one of form 8n±3 divides 2^p+1, and begins an analogous theorem for 3^p−1.

items.quote: Si numerus primus $2p+1$ fuerit formae $8n\pm 1$, per eum semper diuisibilis erit formula $2^p-1$; sin autem habeat hanc formam: $8n\pm 3$, per eum diuisibilis erit formula $2^p+1$.
items.english: If the prime number 2p+1 is of the form 8n±1, the formula 2^p−1 will always be divisible by it; but if it has the form 8n±3, the formula 2^p+1 will be divisible by it.

items.quote: quod eo magis notatu dignum videtur, quod firma demonstratione etiamnum indiget.
items.english: which seems all the more noteworthy because it still lacks a firm demonstration.

items.quote: Si numerus primus $2p+1$ fuerit formae $12n\pm 1$, per eum semper diuisibilis erit formula $3^p-1$.
items.english: If the prime number 2p+1 is of the form 12n±1, the formula 3^p−1 will always be divisible by it.
